source.title: DELMAN: Dynamic Defense Against Large Language Model Jailbreaking with Model Editing
source.authors: Yi Wang; Fenghua Weng; Sibei Yang; Zhan Qin; Minlie Huang; Wenjie Wang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports attack-success rates for jailbreak attacks, including optimized suffix attacks, on aligned models; this bears on whether attacks bypass safety, but it does not use the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position methods.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are the Original Model ASRs in Table 8 for GCG, AutoDAN, and PAIR across four datasets and five models. GCG and AutoDAN are described as optimization-based attacks that search for adversarial suffixes; PAIR rewrites prompts. The paper also reports edited-model and other-defense results, but the rows below isolate the unedited-model attack outcomes. It does not measure refusal rates after benign or harmful fine-tuning, per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, decoding changes, or safety localization.
record.test_reason: This is a jailbreak-defense (model-editing) paper. Its unedited 'Original Model' baselines report how often GCG and AutoDAN adversarial-suffix attacks get compliance from five instruct models on four benchmarks. Those rates bear on V4's claim that suffix attacks defeat refusal, measured in new models and benchmarks. It is weak evidence: there is no no-attack baseline ASR, and the paper does not examine the response opening or position.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. DELMAN's targeted edits sharply cut jailbreak ASR across attacks and datasets, preserve utility, generalize to unseen datasets and behaviors, and support consecutive edits.
record.recipe_differences: This paper evaluates model-editing defenses against jailbreak attacks, not the original sources’ fine-tuning interventions or per-token KL measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type and model matter: the paper says PAIR has little effect on Llama2 and Llama3.1 because they already show strong safety alignment; reported original-model ASRs also vary across datasets and attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: Editing only two MLP down-projection layers (DELMAN) cuts jailbreak ASR to near 0 while keeping utility. This adds refusal rather than locating the model's existing safety.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal against jailbreaks can be installed by rank-limited edits to a few MLP layers keyed on harmful tokens.

record.problems: The listed attack-success results have no reported uncertainty estimates. The authors note evaluations are limited to general-purpose models, larger-scale and specialized models remain untested, GPT-4 is used for token extraction and context generation, and consecutive-edit stability needs deeper analysis.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row cap, retained the Original Model ASRs from Appendix D.1, Table 8 for the five main models and omitted ASRs for LoRA, SafeDecoding, LED, and DELMAN in that table, as well as the additional-model results in Table 9 and behavior-specific or cross-behavior figure results. The omitted edited-defense results concern the paper’s defense intervention rather than the unedited-model attack outcome cataloged here.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant opening, decoding changes, and any link between attack success and the first response tokens. No no-attack ASR is given, so the suffix's added effect over direct requests is unknown.
Localization of existing safety is not tested. DELMAN adds refusal by editing a few MLP layers.

record.verdict_notes: This is a defense paper; the V4-relevant numbers are baselines only. Table 9 (declared as left out) gives further GCG original-model ASRs. Llama-2-13b has 14–18%, which would add to limits_scope. Qwen3-8B has 38–90% and Qwen2.5-14B has 42–93%. ASR is judged by the HarmBench classifier, with default system prompts (the Llama2 prompt is a safety system prompt).

versions.untested_parts: No test of harmful fine-tuning on safety-trained models or refusal/compliance rates after such fine-tuning.
No test of ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning.
No measurement of per-token KL divergence or its distribution across response positions.
Tests optimized suffix attacks (GCG and AutoDAN) and prompt rewriting (PAIR), but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
No test of whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
No test of why safety behavior would be shallow or how training data/objectives produce shallowness.
No test of training that spreads safety beyond initial response tokens or whether such training holds up.
